Seeing What Matters, Verifying What Pays

Load-Adaptive Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models

面向视觉语言模型的负载自适应投机解码

PaperCodeHomePage

A vision-language model emits one token per forward pass, and every pass runs over a long, image-dominated context. Uni-LaSpec lets a block-parallel drafter guess 15 tokens at once and has the model check them in a single pass. It does two things: in every round it shows the drafter the image region the current block actually depends on, and it decides how many candidates to verify, and in what structure, from the current GPU load. Every committed token is checked by the verifier, so the output distribution is unchanged.

01 · Problem

Two places where speculative decoding stalls on VLMs

Speculative speed is set by two quantities: the mean acceptance length \(\tau\) and the cost of each draft–verify round. For a linear draft of \(\gamma\) candidates, the per-token latency is

\[\bar{C}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{draft}}]+\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{ver}}(1+\gamma)]}{\tau},\qquad \tau=\mathbb{E}[a]+1\]

Where should the drafter look?

A text-only drafter never sees the image, so it cannot guess the names, addresses and digit strings that OCR outputs are made of. Feeding it every visual token of a high-resolution page is too expensive: for a block drafter, conditioning on one more visual token costs more than drafting one more token. Yet a 15-token block usually depends on a small region of the image.

So the drafter needs, in every round and at low cost, the evidence this block depends on.

How many candidates should a round verify?

While the verifier is memory-bound, extra positions are inexpensive, and a draft tree that explores alternatives raises \(\tau\). Once load pushes it into the compute-bound regime, every extra position slows every request in the batch, and drafts that will be rejected should be cut.

So the structure and length of verification should follow the load rather than stay fixed.

02 · Method overview

What happens in one decoding round

Uni-LaSpec has two complementary paths. Path I raises the chance that each candidate survives, by showing the drafter the right visual evidence and training it on the accepted prefix. Path II decides where verifier compute goes: trees under low load, dynamically truncated linear drafts under high load. Here is one round in execution order.

03 · Path I · Draft quality

Look where the verifier is already looking

When the verifier produced the current root \(x_j\), its query \(Q_{j-1}\) at every layer attended over all visual keys, and that attention points at the region the next tokens will be read from. The keys were computed at prefill and the query during the last verification, so reading this signal needs no new network and no wait for another forward pass.

View

Follow token by token

MeasuredQwen3.5-4B verifier; the card is resized to 1152 × 704, one visual token per 32 px (22 × 36 = 792 tokens). Selector layers are the full-attention layers 11, 19 and 27. Each nominates 128 tokens by int8 score; tokens are ranked by vote count with mean score breaking ties, and the top k go to the drafter. Click a field on the right, or use “Follow token by token” to watch the selection move along the address and phone number as they are written.

Making the re-scoring cheap

Serving engines compute attention with tiled, fused kernels that never return the scores, so the scores have to be recomputed. Three choices keep that under a millisecond.

Rank only. Selection uses the order of the scores, never their values, so the softmax is skipped. int8 visual keys. Keys are cached once per request in 8-bit form with one scale per position and key head, halving memory and traffic. Average queries per GQA group. The G query heads that share a key head are averaged before the dot product, so H dot products replace GH. On the drafter side, a gated cross-attention reads only the k selected tokens. Its gate starts at zero, and training decides how far to open it. Fusing scoring, voting, gathering and cross-attention into one execution also removes launch and synchronization overhead: on Q3.5-4B/9B the selector stays below 1 ms at every measured load (0.38–0.94 ms), 2.58–18.04× faster than unfused full scoring.

\[\tilde{c}_i=\mathrm{RMSNorm}\big(c_i+g\cdot\mathrm{XA}(c_i,\,V_{\mathcal{S}_j})\big),\qquad g\ \text{initialized to}\ 0\]

Without re-selection every round, the visual branch sits empty

vLLM exposes image embeddings only in the step that schedules them. After prefill, decoding windows contain no visual tokens, so a drafter’s visual branch would be idle for the whole generation. Uni-LaSpec caches the image embeddings per request and re-selects the top-k with the verifier’s last retained query in every round, so the drafter can read visual evidence throughout.

Train the drafter on the accepted prefix

A round is paid for in accepted prefix: an error at position i does not cost one token, it voids everything after it. Positions are not interchangeable, so the loss weights each one by \(w_i\), the expected number of tokens accepted from position i onward. This is also the sensitivity of the expected accepted length to that position’s accuracy.

\[\bar{q}_i=(1-\alpha)\,e^{-\mathrm{CE}_i}+\alpha,\qquad w_i=\sum_{v=i}^{\Gamma}\prod_{t=1}^{v}\bar{q}_t\]
Position weight \(w_i\) (relative to uniform)Accuracy at that position \(e^{-\mathrm{CE}}\)Uniform weighting

IllustrativeThe accuracy curve is an assumed decay with depth; \(\alpha=0.5\) is the value used in training. The weights spend gradient on early positions and on positions the drafter nearly gets right, and stop chasing deep positions that are already unreachable.

04 · Path II · Load-adaptive verification

Is one more candidate worth verifying?

Add a candidate whose parent prefix is already kept and whose survival probability is \(\pi\). With drafting cost held fixed, throughput improves if and only if

\[\pi>\delta(W)\triangleq\frac{R\,\bar{\tau}\,\big[C_{\mathrm{ver}}(W{+}1)-C_{\mathrm{ver}}(W)\big]}{C_{\mathrm{draft}}+C_{\mathrm{ver}}(W)}\]

While verification is memory-bound, the marginal cost is near zero and \(\delta\approx 0\), so extra candidates are inexpensive. Past the knee \(W^{*}\) of the cost curve, \(\delta\) rises and expansion becomes selective. Drag the request count to see what the scheduler picks.

IllustrativeThe cost curve’s shape is schematic; the knee \(W^{*}=64\) matches the paper’s R=5 scheduling trace. The tree budget is the largest of {63, 31, 15} that fits under the knee. The linear threshold profile is the 0.25 / 0.45 / 0.6 / 0.6 profile (at widths 64 / 128 / 256 / 512) from the paper’s bursty-arrival run, chosen at a self-consistent width. Draft length assumes survival \(\hat{\rho}_i=0.85^{i}\), with \(\Delta=1\) slack and five buckets.

Low load: grow a tree with idle verifier width

One pass of the block drafter yields a full distribution at every position, and a linear draft uses only each position’s top-1. Given the root, the per-position marginals are independent, so a candidate continuation is just a choice of rank at each depth, valued at the product of its probabilities. Value only falls along a path, so the B most valuable prefixes always form a tree, grown by best-first expansion.

Attention mask (row = query node, column = visible node)

IllustrativeContext “The cat has just”, root token “sat”; the top-3 marginals per depth are made-up values. The verifier’s true continuation is “on the floor .”: the linear draft “on the mat .” breaks at position 3, but once the tree contains the “floor” branch, a single verification accepts two more tokens. Each node sees only the cached history, its ancestors and itself, and its rotary position is j + depth.

High load: truncate linear drafts by predicted survival

Under high load, deep block positions are mostly verified only to be rejected, and every request in the batch pays for that waste. A fixed width does not fix it either: a request in the middle of a predictable phrase can be drafted far ahead, while one at a genuinely uncertain point should barely be drafted. A shared dynamic head reads out the drafter’s own confidence \(\hat{\rho}_i\); each request keeps the longest prefix with \(\hat{\rho}_i\ge\delta(W)\), relaxed one-sidedly (\(+\Delta\), rounded up to a bucket edge) so that an underestimate costs a little verifier width rather than accepted tokens.

Trees and linear drafts share one batch

The structure is not fixed at drafting time. One drafter pass keeps the greedy chain, per-position alternatives and the dynamic-head estimates; when a request is admitted to a verifier batch, the scheduler gives it a tree, a truncated linear prefix, or only its root, based on that batch’s actual load. A mixed mask lets tree nodes see only their ancestors and linear nodes their causal prefix, and keeps requests invisible to each other. Below is the real round-by-round trace of Qwen3.5-4B at client concurrency R=5: with four requests decoding, 4 × (1+15) = 64 fits the knee and trees are used; with all five decoding, the scheduler switches to truncated linear drafts. Rounds that share the batch with a prefill chunk are verified linearly as well, because the chunk consumes part of the token budget.

05 · Results

Six verifiers, seventeen benchmarks, six load levels

The verifiers are Qwen3.5-4B/9B (Q3.5), InternVL3.5-4B/8B (IVL3.5) and Gemma 4 E2B/E4B (G4). Seven text benchmarks cover math, code and dialogue; ten multimodal benchmarks cover documents, charts, visual reasoning, captioning and dialogue. Each benchmark supplies at most 100 prompts, outputs are capped at 1024 tokens, and the drafter predicts \(\Gamma=15\) positions.

Uni-LaSpec raises acceptance on every verifier

Verifier

MeasuredMean accepted length \(\tau\) per benchmark at R=1, T=0, with full-width linear verification (no trees, no truncation). DFlash (T)/(M) use the same block-drafter architecture without direct visual input, trained on text-only and on the full multimodal mixture; EAGLE-3 is available for the two Qwen3.5 verifiers only. The right column is Uni-LaSpec’s change relative to DFlash (M). MTP uses the full 248,320-token vocabulary and is not directly comparable with compressed-vocabulary drafters, so it is not plotted. Across both temperatures, Uni-LaSpec exceeds DFlash (M) on 198 of 204 entries. EAGLE-3 and MTP draft autoregressively, paying one drafter step per position, so a long accepted length does not by itself yield speed: on GSM8K with Q3.5-4B at T=0, MTP accepts 6.11 tokens against 5.35 for Uni-LaSpec, yet reaches 1.68× AR throughput against 3.58×. Block-parallel drafting fills the whole block in one pass, at a cost nearly independent of its length.

Where a round’s time goes

Each bar is one draft–verify round of a verification strategy, split into segments in execution order and divided by that strategy’s \(\tau\) to give time per output token; shorter is faster. Switch concurrency, granularity and clock.

Under bursty traffic, the queue recovers sooner

420 requests arrive over 250 s on one open-loop Poisson trace, with at most 32 in flight. Latency runs from arrival to completion and includes waiting at the client. On this trace the mean is 14.0 s for Uni-LaSpec, 26.74 s for Linear, 33.09 s for Tree B=15 and 84.13 s for Tree B=31: fixed trees accept more tokens but build a backlog during the burst, which makes the later spike more expensive.

MeasuredInteractive version of paper Fig. 12 · Qwen3.5-4B

With the vocabulary limit removed: business models

The compressed vocabulary keeps the 32,768 most frequent tokens of the drafter’s training responses, while OCR outputs transcribe what the document prints: names, identifiers, formulas, and languages rare in those responses. On OmniDocBench, 13.5–19.5% of output tokens fall outside it (3.5–4.6% for multimodal outputs overall), and each such token ends the accepted prefix. Here, two verifiers fine-tuned on in-house business data for schema-guided medical-document extraction use full-vocabulary drafters (248,320 tokens, three auxiliary layers), with 100 held-out prompts and outputs capped at 4096 tokens. Uni-LaSpec accepts 9.92 tokens per round, against 5.55–5.66 for MTP. An autoregressive drafter would ordinarily predict more accurately, but the MTP drafter of Qwen3.5 is a single layer applied recurrently with shared weights, whereas the block drafter has six layers and reads features fused from several verifier layers.

06 · Conclusion

Acceptance and speed have to be read together

Uni-LaSpec couples visual evidence selection with load-adaptive verification for block-parallel VLM drafting. Across six VLMs and 17 benchmarks, it raises acceptance over the same block drafter without direct visual input on 198 of 204 benchmark entries, and selecting eight visual tokens retains nearly all of the accepted length obtained from the complete image while keeping selection below one millisecond. Acceptance and speed must be optimized together: larger trees accept more tokens but lose throughput under load, whereas truncation pays off as concurrency rises. By choosing the structure per request and per round, the load-adaptive policy improves on autoregressive decoding in every evaluated setting and matches or exceeds the best fixed strategy in 123 of the 144 evaluated model–modality–load settings. Under bursty arrivals, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by 47.6% relative to linear verification.
